Content:
We've seen how to calculate probabilities for normally distributed random variables [MATH: X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)] when [MATH: \mu] and [MATH: \sigma^2] are both known.

Content:
In this lesson, we'll learn how to calculate the mean [MATH: \mu] or the variance [MATH: \sigma^2] of a normally distributed random variable when given a specific probability.

Content:
For example, suppose we have a normally distributed random variable [MATH: X] with unknown mean [MATH: {\color{blue}\mu}] and known variance [MATH: {\color{red}{\sigma}}^2 = {\color{red}2}^2.] We write this as follows:

Content:
[MATH: X \sim N({\color{blue}\mu}, {\color{red}2}^2)]

Content:
Now, suppose we also know that

Content:
[MATH: P(X \leq 2.1) = 0.7088.]

Content:
We can use this additional information about [MATH: X] to calculate the mean [MATH: {\color{blue}\mu}.]

Content:
First, we transform to a standard normal random variable [MATH: Z\sim N(0,1)] by [MATH: z]-scoring:

Content:
[MATH: Z = \dfrac{X - \mu}{\sigma}]

Content:
Applying the [MATH: z]-scoring transformation to our probability statement, we get the following:

Content:
[MATH: P(X ≤ 2.1)|= 0.7088; P((X − μ)/(σ) ≤ (2.1 − μ)/(σ))|= 0.7088; P(Z ≤ (2.1 − μ)/(σ))|= 0.7088]

Content:
Substituting [MATH: {\color{red}{\sigma}} = {\color{red}{2}},] we get
[MATH: P\left(Z \leq \dfrac{2.1 - {\color{blue}{\mu}}}{\color{red}{2}}\right) = 0.7088.]

Content:
Now, using the fact that [MATH: P(Z\leq z) = \Phi(z),] where [MATH: \Phi] is the cumulative distribution function of [MATH: Z,] we can write the above statement as follows:
[MATH: \Phi\left(\dfrac{2.1 - {\color{blue}{\mu}}}{2}\right) = 0.7088 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \Phi^{-1}(0.7088) = \dfrac{2.1 - {\color{blue}{\mu}}}{2}]

Content:
Let's now take a look at the table of values for [MATH: \Phi(z).]

[MATH: \Phi(0.55) = 0.7088 \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad \Phi^{-1}( 0.7088) = 0.55.]

[MATH: (2.1 − μ)/(2)|= 0.55; 2.1 − μ|= 1.1; μ|= 1]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
We've seen how to calculate probabilities for normally distributed random variables [MATH: X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)] when [MATH: \mu] and [MATH: \sigma^2] are both known.

Content:
In this lesson, we'll learn how to calculate the mean [MATH: \mu] or the variance [MATH: \sigma^2] of a normally distributed random variable when given a specific probability.

Content:
For example, suppose we have a normally distributed random variable [MATH: X] with unknown mean [MATH: {\color{blue}\mu}] and known variance [MATH: {\color{red}{\sigma}}^2 = {\color{red}2}^2.] We write this as follows:

Content:
[MATH: X \sim N({\color{blue}\mu}, {\color{red}2}^2)]

Content:
Now, suppose we also know that

Content:
[MATH: P(X \leq 2.1) = 0.7088.]

Content:
We can use this additional information about [MATH: X] to calculate the mean [MATH: {\color{blue}\mu}.]

Content:
First, we transform to a standard normal random variable [MATH: Z\sim N(0,1)] by [MATH: z]-scoring:

Content:
[MATH: Z = \dfrac{X - \mu}{\sigma}]

Content:
Applying the [MATH: z]-scoring transformation to our probability statement, we get the following:

Content:
[MATH: P(X ≤ 2.1)|= 0.7088; P((X − μ)/(σ) ≤ (2.1 − μ)/(σ))|= 0.7088; P(Z ≤ (2.1 − μ)/(σ))|= 0.7088]

Content:
Substituting [MATH: {\color{red}{\sigma}} = {\color{red}{2}},] we get
[MATH: P\left(Z \leq \dfrac{2.1 - {\color{blue}{\mu}}}{\color{red}{2}}\right) = 0.7088.]

Content:
Now, using the fact that [MATH: P(Z\leq z) = \Phi(z),] where [MATH: \Phi] is the cumulative distribution function of [MATH: Z,] we can write the above statement as follows:
[MATH: \Phi\left(\dfrac{2.1 - {\color{blue}{\mu}}}{2}\right) = 0.7088 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \Phi^{-1}(0.7088) = \dfrac{2.1 - {\color{blue}{\mu}}}{2}]

Content:
Let's now take a look at the table of values for [MATH: \Phi(z).]

Content:
| [MATH: z] | [MATH: \, 0.03 \,] | [MATH: \, 0.04 \,] | [MATH: \, 0.05 \,] |
| [MATH: \, 0.4 \,] | [MATH: \, 0.6664 \,] | [MATH: \, 0.6700 \,] | [MATH: \, 0.6736 \,] |

| [MATH: \, 0.6 \,] | [MATH: \, 0.7357 \,] | [MATH: \, 0.7389 \,] | [MATH: \, 0.7422 \,] |

Content:
According to the table, we have

Content:
[MATH: \Phi(0.55) = 0.7088 \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad \Phi^{-1}( 0.7088) = 0.55.]

Content:
Equating our two expressions for [MATH: \Phi^{-1}( 0.7088),] we can now solve for [MATH: \mu] as follows:

Content:
[MATH: (2.1 − μ)/(2)|= 0.55; 2.1 − μ|= 1.1; μ|= 1]

Then, we transform to a standard normal random variable by [MATH: z]-scoring:

Item 8 — Tutorial: Using Symmetry Properties

Content:
It's often helpful to use the symmetry properties of the normal distribution to help us determine unknown parameters.

Content:
For example, suppose we have the following normal random variable with unknown variance [MATH: \sigma^2{:}]

Content:
[MATH: X \sim N(1, \sigma^2)]

Content:
Suppose we also know that

Content:
[MATH: P(-2 \lt X \lt 4) = 0.8714.]

Content:
The interval [MATH: -2 \lt X \lt 4] and the area associated with the probability that [MATH: X] lies within this interval are shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/ce94488a86458c4f936020feb0b2630f]

Content:
The endpoints of the interval [MATH: (-2,4)] both lie at a distance of [MATH: {\color{red}{3}}] from the mean [MATH: \mu.] So, this interval is symmetric about the mean, and we can write the given probability as follows:
[MATH: P(\mu - {\color{red}{3}} \lt X \lt \mu + {\color{red}{3}}) = 0.8714]

Content:
By symmetry, the total shaded equals twice the area between the mean [MATH: \mu] and the right endpoint:
[MATH: 2P(\mu < X < \mu + 3) = 0.8714]

Content:
Dividing this equation by [MATH: 2,] we get

Content:
[MATH: P(\mu < X < \mu + 3) = 0.4357.]

Content:
Let's write this probability in terms of [MATH: Z\sim N(0,1)] by [MATH: z]-scoring:

Content:
[MATH: P((μ − μ)/(σ) < (X − μ)/(σ) < (μ + 3 − μ)/(σ)) = 0.4357]

Content:
This simplifies to

Content:
[MATH: P(0 < Z < (3)/(σ)) = 0.4357.]

Content:
Writing this in terms of [MATH: \Phi,] we have

Content:
[MATH: \Phi\left(\dfrac{3}{\sigma}\right) - \Phi(0) = 0.4357]

Content:
